analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the federal estate and gift taxes was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in February 2013 and never received a hearing or vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the federal estate tax (the tax owed when someone dies and leaves a very large estate), along with the gift tax and the tax on certain transfers that skip a generation. The estate tax applies only to estates above a large exemption — over $5 million per person in 2013 — so repeal would exclusively benefit the heirs of the wealthiest households, while removing billions of dollars a year in federal revenue. The bill was introduced, referred to the tax-writing committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates large enough to owe the estate tax — a small share of estates, those exceeding roughly $5.25 million per person in 2013 — would keep the entire estate instead of paying the tax. Wealthy individuals making large lifetime gifts would also avoid gift tax. The bill's title points to farm families, but farm and small-business estates already qualify for high exemptions and special payment rules, so the largest dollar savings go to the biggest fortunes.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and transfers occurring after enactment.

Because the estate tax exempts the first several million dollars of an estate and applies only above that threshold, the money saved under repeal would go overwhelmingly to heirs of the wealthiest households.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would lose the estate and gift tax revenue — tens of billions of dollars per year in the years the bill was pending — which either means larger deficits or higher taxes or lower spending elsewhere that falls on everyone else.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers and the federal Treasury

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate and gift taxes removes a major federal revenue source; the lost money would have to be replaced with other taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts affecting the general public.

The repeal is not targeted at small farms: the estate tax already exempts estates up to roughly $5.25 million per person in 2013 and allows special deferral and payment terms for qualifying farm and business estates, so the benefits concentrate at the top rather than rescuing family farms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are enormous but concentrated in a very small number of very wealthy families, while the costs — lost revenue forcing other taxes, more debt, or cuts — are spread across everyone. Framed around farms, the bill's actual largest beneficiaries would be heirs of multi-million-dollar estates.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Hudson (R-NC) introduced the bill on February 4, 2013.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation.
Sixty-three members cosponsored the bill: 61 Republicans and 2 Democrats.
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers in general are better off that the bill died, because the estate tax continues to collect revenue from a few thousand large estates each year rather than being eliminated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the estate tax stayed on the books

industries.industry: Heirs of large estates (households above the estate-tax threshold)
industries.note: Repeal would let these heirs keep the full estate instead of paying tax on the portion above roughly $5 million per person; the tax they avoid would be replaced by deficits or taxes on everyone else.

industries.industry: Estate planning, trusts, and wealth advisory services
industries.note: Repealing the estate and gift taxes would shrink demand for the complex planning these firms sell to dodge the taxes; they are not a public antagonist but their business model depends on the tax existing.

The bill is named for them, and repeal would spare some farm heirs from any tax; however, most farm estates were already below the exemption or qualified for deferral, so the direct benefit to ordinary farm families is smaller than the title suggests.
